Hashing and Verifying with bcrypt

One function to hash a password on write, one to check a guess against that hash on login — never the reverse.

utils/password.js is two thin wrappers around the bcrypt package, reused everywhere this project touches a password:

// Figure 4.1: hashing and verifying (src/utils/password.js)
import bcrypt from 'bcrypt';

const SALT_ROUNDS = 10;

export const hashPassword = async (plainPassword) => bcrypt.hash(plainPassword, SALT_ROUNDS);

export const verifyPassword = async (plainPassword, hash) => bcrypt.compare(plainPassword, hash);

hashPassword is one-way, deliberately: there is no unhashPassword, and bcrypt doesn't offer one — a hash can't be turned back into the password that produced it. That's the whole point: even this project's own code, and anyone who ever reads the database directly, can only ever compare a guess against a stored hash, never recover the real password from it. verifyPassword is that comparison — bcrypt.compare re-hashes the guess internally and checks whether the result matches, so this project's own code never needs to (and never could) reverse a stored hash to check it.

SALT_ROUNDS controls how many times bcrypt repeats its own hashing work internally — a deliberately slow operation, not an accident of a naive implementation. That slowness is the actual security property: it's what makes guessing passwords against a stolen hash (trying millions of candidates) expensive enough to be impractical, while a single real login attempt (one hash, one comparison) still feels instant to a user. 10 is bcrypt's own long-standing recommended default, balancing that cost against how long a real login should ever take to check.
